title: Graphs of Sine, Cosine, and Tangent Functions
overview: Trigonometric ratios grow up into **trigonometric functions**. You will graph $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$ and $y=\tan x$ using radian measure, describe their key properties, and see how each constant in $y=\sin x+c$, $y=a\sin x$, $y=\sin(x-d)$ and $y=\sin kx$ changes the graph. These graphs model sound, electricity and theme-park rides.
objectives: Sketch $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ in radians and state their amplitude, period, zeros, domain and range.
Graph $y=\tan x$, explain its asymptotes and describe its key properties.
Describe the effect of $c$, $a$, $d$ and $k$ on the graphs of sine and cosine.
Use $T=\frac{2\pi}{k}$ to move between period and $k$.
Write equations for sinusoidal functions from a description and model simple periodic situations.
Classify the trigonometric functions as even or odd.

lessons.title: From ratios to functions
lessons.body:
In earlier courses you used $\sin\theta$, $\cos\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ as **ratios** of sides in a right triangle. Now we treat them as **functions**: feed in *any* real number $x$ (an angle in **radians**) and get out a value.

Think of a point moving around the **unit circle** (radius 1). After it turns through an angle $x$:

* its $y$-coordinate is $\sin x$
* its $x$-coordinate is $\cos x$
* the slope of the radius is $\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$

Because the point returns to the same place every full turn ($2\pi$ rad), the values repeat. Functions whose values repeat at regular intervals are called **periodic**.

### Special-angle values you should know

| $x$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ | $\pi$ | $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ | $2\pi$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin x$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\approx0.71$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx0.87$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ |
| $\cos x$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| $\tan x$ | $0$ | $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\approx0.58$ | $1$ | $\sqrt3\approx1.73$ | undefined | $0$ | undefined | $0$ |

> **Calculator check:** always switch to **Radian mode** in this chapter. $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}$ should give $0.5$.

lessons.title: The graph of y = sin x
lessons.body:
Plot the table values and join them with a smooth wave:


```plot
title: y = sin x
f: sin(x) | label=y = sin x
domain: -2*pi, 2*pi
range: -1.5, 1.5
xticks: pi
points: (0,0), (pi/2,1), (pi,0), (3*pi/2,-1), (2*pi,0)
```


**Key features of $y=\sin x$**

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| Maximum / minimum | $1$ (at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi$) / $-1$ (at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}+2n\pi$) |
| Amplitude | $1$ (half the distance from max to min) |
| Period | $2\pi$ |
| Zeros in $[0,2\pi]$ | $0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$ |
| $y$-intercept | $0$ |
| Domain / range | $\{x\in\mathbb R\}$ / $\{y\in\mathbb R \mid -1\le y\le 1\}$ |

**The five key points.** One cycle of a sine wave always contains: a zero, a maximum, a zero, a minimum and a zero, spaced a **quarter period** apart. Sketching becomes easy once you place these five points.

lessons.title: The graph of y = cos x
lessons.body:
```plot
title: y = sin x (dashed) and y = cos x
f: cos(x) | label=y = cos x
f: sin(x) | dashed; label=y = sin x
domain: -2*pi, 2*pi
range: -1.5, 1.5
xticks: pi
points: (0,1), (pi/2,0), (pi,-1), (3*pi/2,0), (2*pi,1)
```


The cosine graph has **exactly the same shape** as the sine graph – it is just shifted.

| Feature | $y=\cos x$ |
|---|---|
| Maximum / minimum | $1$ at $x=0,\,2\pi,\dots$ / $-1$ at $x=\pi,\,3\pi,\dots$ |
| Amplitude / period | $1$ / $2\pi$ |
| Zeros in $[0,2\pi]$ | $\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3\pi}{2}$ |
| $y$-intercept | $1$ |
| Domain / range | $\{x\in\mathbb R\}$ / $\{y\mid -1\le y\le1\}$ |

**Linking the two graphs:** shifting $y=\sin x$ to the **left** by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ gives $y=\cos x$:
$$\cos x=\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sin x=\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$$
Because both graphs repeat every $2\pi$, there are infinitely many phase shifts that work (e.g. $\frac{\pi}{2}-2\pi=-\frac{3\pi}{2}$ to the right also maps sine onto cosine).

**Even and odd.** $\cos(-x)=\cos x$, so cosine is an **even** function (symmetric in the $y$-axis). $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, so sine is **odd** (rotational symmetry about the origin).

lessons.title: The graph of y = tan x
lessons.body:
Since $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$, tangent is **undefined wherever $\cos x=0$**, that is at $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2},\dots$ (odd multiples of $\frac{\pi}{2}$).

What happens near $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$?

* Just to the **left** ($x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^-$): $\sin x\approx1$ and $\cos x$ is a tiny **positive** number, so $\tan x\to+\infty$.
* Just to the **right** ($x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^+$): $\cos x$ is a tiny **negative** number, so $\tan x\to-\infty$.

The graph therefore has **vertical asymptotes** at these values.


```plot
title: y = tan x
f: tan(x) | label=y = tan x
domain: -2*pi, 2*pi
range: -6, 6
xticks: pi
asymptote x: -3*pi/2, -pi/2, pi/2, 3*pi/2
points: (0,0), (pi/4,1), (pi,0), (-pi/4,-1)
```


| Feature | $y=\tan x$ |
|---|---|
| Max / min / amplitude | none – the graph is unbounded, so **no amplitude** |
| Period | $\pi$ |
| Zeros in $[0,2\pi]$ | $0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$ |
| Asymptotes in $[0,2\pi]$ | $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\ x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$ |
| Domain | $\{x\in\mathbb R \mid x\ne\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi,\ n\in\mathbb Z\}$ |
| Range | $\{y\in\mathbb R\}$ |

Tangent is **odd**: $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$. It is still a function – every vertical line meets the graph at most once.

lessons.title: One transformation at a time
lessons.body:
Each constant in a transformed sine or cosine function does **one job**. Learn them separately first.

| Equation | Effect on $y=\sin x$ | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| $y=\sin x+c$ | vertical translation $c$ units (up if $c>0$) | max $=1+c$, min $=-1+c$ |
| $y=a\sin x$ | vertical stretch by $\lvert a\rvert$; reflection in the $x$-axis if $a<0$ | amplitude $=\lvert a\rvert$ |
| $y=\sin(x-d)$ | horizontal translation (**phase shift**) $d$ units (right if $d>0$) | zeros move to $x=d,\ d+\pi,\dots$ |
| $y=\sin kx$ | horizontal compression/stretch by factor $\frac1k$ | period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{k}$ |

The same rules apply to $y=\cos x$ (and $c$, $a$, $d$, $k$ act on $y=\tan x$ the same way, except that tangent has period $\frac{\pi}{k}$ and no amplitude).


```plot
title: y = sin x, y = 2 sin x and y = sin 2x
f: sin(x) | dashed; label=y = sin x
f: 2*sin(x) | label=y = 2 sin x
f: sin(2*x) | label=y = sin 2x
domain: 0, 2*pi
range: -2.5, 2.5
xticks: pi
```


**Watch the sign of $d$.** In $y=\sin(x-d)$, the zero that used to be at $x=0$ now happens when $x-d=0$, i.e. at $x=d$. So
* $y=\sin\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ shifts **right** $\frac{\pi}{4}$
* $y=\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\sin\left(x-\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)$ shifts **left** $\frac{\pi}{6}$

**Period and $k$.** Bigger $k$ means more cycles squeezed into the same space, so a **shorter** period. Solving for $k$: $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\text{period}}$.

**Frequency.** In physics, the **frequency** $f$ (in hertz, Hz) is the number of cycles per second. It is the reciprocal of the period: $f=\dfrac{1}{T}$. For $y=\sin kt$, $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f$.

keyTerms.definition: A function whose values repeat at regular intervals: $f(x+p)=f(x)$ for every $x$, where $p$ is the period.
The horizontal length of one complete cycle. For $y=\sin kx$ or $y=\cos kx$ it is $\frac{2\pi}{k}$; for $y=\tan kx$ it is $\frac{\pi}{k}$.
Half the distance between the maximum and minimum values: $\frac{\max-\min}{2}$. For $y=a\sin x$ it is $\lvert a\rvert$. Tangent has no amplitude.
A horizontal translation of a sinusoidal graph. In $y=\sin(x-d)$ the phase shift is $d$ (right if $d>0$, left if $d<0$).
The constant $c$ in $y=\sin x+c$; it moves the whole graph up or down and sets the midline $y=c$.
Any function whose graph is a transformed sine or cosine wave.
A vertical line $x=a$ that the graph approaches but never reaches; $y=\tan x$ has one wherever $\cos x=0$.
The number of cycles completed per unit of time (cycles per second = hertz). Frequency $=\frac{1}{\text{period}}$.

formulas.meaning: Read straight from the highest and lowest values.

formulas.meaning: Explains the zeros and asymptotes of the tangent graph.

workedExamples.title: Vertical translations
workedExamples.problem: Predict the maximum and minimum values of $y=\sin x+2$ and $y=\sin x-3$ and where they occur on $[0,2\pi]$.
steps: Adding a constant changes every $y$-coordinate by the same amount – a vertical translation.
$y=\sin x$ has max $1$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and min $-1$ at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

$y=\sin x-3$: max $-2$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$; min $-4$ at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

```plot
f: sin(x) | dashed; label=y = sin x
f: sin(x)+2 | label=y = sin x + 2
f: sin(x)-3 | label=y = sin x − 3
domain: 0, 2*pi
range: -4.5, 3.5
xticks: pi
```
workedExamples.answer: The $x$-values of the max and min do not change; only the heights move by $c$.

workedExamples.title: Amplitude and reflection
steps: $a=-3$: amplitude $\lvert -3\rvert=3$, and the negative sign reflects the graph in the $x$-axis.

Multiply each $y$-coordinate by $-3$: $(0,0),(\frac{\pi}{2},-3),(\pi,0),(\frac{3\pi}{2},3),(2\pi,0)$.

```plot
f: sin(x) | dashed; label=y = sin x
f: -3*sin(x) | label=y = −3 sin x
domain: 0, 2*pi
range: -3.5, 3.5
xticks: pi
points: (pi/2,-3), (3*pi/2,3)
```
workedExamples.answer: Amplitude 3, max $3$ at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$, min $-3$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$; zeros unchanged.

workedExamples.title: Phase shift
steps: The graph of $y=\sin x$ is shifted $\frac{\pi}{4}$ to the **right**.
Zeros of $\sin x$ are at $0,\pi,2\pi$. Add $\frac{\pi}{4}$: $\frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{5\pi}{4},\ \frac{9\pi}{4}$.
$\frac{9\pi}{4}>2\pi$, so discard it. Check the left end: the zero at $-\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}=-\frac{3\pi}{4}$ is outside too.

workedExamples.title: Changing the period
workedExamples.problem: State the period of $y=\sin 2x$ and $y=\sin\frac12 x$.
steps: Use $T=\frac{2\pi}{k}$.
$y=\sin2x$: $T=\frac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$ – the graph is compressed horizontally (two cycles in $2\pi$).
$y=\sin\frac12x$: $T=\frac{2\pi}{1/2}=4\pi$ – the graph is stretched horizontally (half a cycle in $2\pi$).

workedExamples.title: Household electricity
workedExamples.problem: The voltage of North American household electricity has a maximum of about $120$ V and a frequency of $60$ Hz. Model it with $V=a\sin kt$.
steps: Amplitude: $a=120$.
Period: $T=\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{60}$ s.
Model: $V=120\sin(120\pi t)$.

workedExamples.title: The Octopus ride
workedExamples.problem: An Octopus ride completes one revolution every $60$ s. Riders reach a maximum height of $4$ m and a minimum of $1$ m. Find $a$, $c$ and $k$ for $h=a\sin(kt)+c$.
steps: $c=\frac{4+1}{2}=2.5$ m (the height of the midline).
Period $60$ s, so $k=\frac{2\pi}{60}=\frac{\pi}{30}$.

misconceptions.myth: The calculator gives weird answers, so the formula must be wrong.
misconceptions.fact: Check the mode first. In this chapter angles are in **radians**; a calculator in degree mode gives $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=\sin(0.5236^\circ)\approx0.009$ instead of $0.5$.

misconceptions.myth: $y=\sin(x+\frac{\pi}{3})$ shifts the graph to the right because of the plus sign.
misconceptions.fact: A **plus** inside the brackets shifts **left**. Write it as $\sin(x-(-\frac{\pi}{3}))$: $d=-\frac{\pi}{3}$.

misconceptions.myth: A larger $k$ gives a longer period.
misconceptions.fact: Period $=\frac{2\pi}{k}$, so a larger $k$ gives a **shorter** period – more cycles in the same interval.
Amplitude is a distance, so it is always positive: $\lvert-2\rvert=2$. The negative sign means a reflection.

misconceptions.myth: The tangent graph has an amplitude of 1 because $\tan\frac{\pi}{4}=1$.
misconceptions.fact: Tangent has **no** maximum or minimum, so it has no amplitude at all.

misconceptions.myth: Tangent has the same period as sine and cosine.

realWorld.title: Sound
realWorld.body: A musical note is a pressure wave. The A above middle C vibrates $440$ times per second (440 Hz), so its period is $\frac{1}{440}\approx0.00227$ s and it can be modelled by $y=\sin(880\pi t)$. Higher notes have larger $k$ and shorter periods.

realWorld.title: Electricity
realWorld.body: The alternating current in your home follows $V=120\sin(120\pi t)$: the voltage swings between $+120$ V and $-120$ V sixty times every second.

realWorld.title: Business cycles
realWorld.body: Economists describe periods of expansion and contraction of the economy with a periodic, wave-like model – a use of trigonometric functions that has nothing to do with triangles.

realWorld.title: Wave pools
realWorld.body: A wave generator pushing back and forth 20 times a minute has a period of $3$ s. The height of the wave from crest to trough is twice the amplitude.

practice.question: State the maximum and minimum values of $y=\cos x-5$ and the values of $x$ in $[-2\pi,2\pi]$ where they occur.
practice.hint: Vertical translation only: subtract 5 from the max and min of $\cos x$.

practice.question: Write an equation of a sine function with amplitude $4$ that is reflected in the $x$-axis.
Write an equation of a cosine function with a phase shift of $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ to the left.
Write an equation of a cosine function with period $\frac{3\pi}{2}$.
One cycle of a sine function begins at $x=-\frac{\pi}{6}$ and ends at $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$. Find the period, the phase shift, and an equation of the form $y=\sin[k(x-d)]$.
practice.hint: Period = end − start. A sine cycle 'begins' at a zero going up.
practice.solution: Period $=\frac{\pi}{3}-(-\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{\pi}{2}$, so $k=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/2}=4$. The cycle starts at $x=-\frac{\pi}{6}$, so the phase shift is $\frac{\pi}{6}$ left: $y=\sin\left[4\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]$.

practice.question: Is $y=\tan x$ even, odd or neither? Justify.
practice.hint: Compare $\tan(-x)$ with $\tan x$ using the quotient identity.
practice.solution: $\tan(-x)=\frac{\sin(-x)}{\cos(-x)}=\frac{-\sin x}{\cos x}=-\tan x$, so tangent is **odd**.

practice.question: A flute note has frequency $440$ Hz. Find its period and the value of $k$ in $y=\sin kt$.
Use the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ to explain why $y=\tan x$ is negative on $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$.
practice.hint: Look at the signs of sine and cosine there.
practice.solution: On $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$, $\sin x>0$ but $\cos x<0$, so the quotient $\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ is negative.

summary: $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$ are periodic with amplitude 1, period $2\pi$, domain $\mathbb R$ and range $[-1,1]$.
$y=\tan x$ has period $\pi$, no amplitude, zeros at $n\pi$, and vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
In $y=a\sin[k(x-d)]+c$: $\lvert a\rvert$ = amplitude, $\frac{2\pi}{k}$ = period, $d$ = phase shift, $c$ = vertical translation.
Frequency is the reciprocal of period.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Adding {{c}} translates every point up {{c}} units, so the maximum is $1+{{c}}={{c+1}}$.

(b) The minimum is $-1+{{c}}={{c-1}}$.

(c) The maximum occurs where $\sin x=1$: $x=-\frac{3\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$. The minimum occurs where $\sin x=-1$: $x=-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$.

(d) Range: $\{y\in\mathbb R \mid {{c-1}}\le y\le {{c+1}}\}$.

rubric.point: Correct x-values for max and min (all four)

parts.label: a

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the minimum value and where it occurs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the graph is related to the graph of $y=\cos x$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Max $=1-{{c}}={{1-c}}$, at $x=0,\ \pm2\pi,\dots$

(b) Min $=-1-{{c}}={{-1-c}}$, at $x=\pm\pi,\ \pm3\pi,\dots$

(c) Every point of $y=\cos x$ moves {{c}} units down; the midline is $y=-{{c}}$. The shape, period ($2\pi$) and amplitude (1) are unchanged.

rubric.point: Correct maximum and where it occurs
Correct minimum and where it occurs
Describes the transformation as a vertical translation down

questions.text: Write an equation for each function and state its maximum and minimum values. (a) a sine function with amplitude {{a}}, reflected in the $x$-axis; (b) a cosine function with amplitude {{b}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sine function, amplitude {{a}}, reflected in the $x$-axis.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Cosine function, amplitude {{b}}.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $y=-{{a}}\sin x$. Reflection changes the sign of $a$ but the amplitude is still {{a}}: max $={{a}}$ (at $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$), min $=-{{a}}$ (at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$).

(b) $y={{b}}\cos x$: max $={{b}}$, min $=-{{b}}$.

questions.text: Write an equation of a sine function with period $\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ and amplitude 1. Then state how many complete cycles it makes on $[0,2\pi]$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine $k$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: How many complete cycles are there on $[0,2\pi]$?

questions.modelAnswer:
Use $k=\frac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/{{n}}}=2({{n}})={{2*n}}$.

Equation: $y=\sin {{2*n}}x$.

Number of cycles in $[0,2\pi]$: $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/{{n}}}={{2*n}}$ cycles.

rubric.point: Correct number of cycles with reasoning

questions.text: A cosine function has a maximum value of {{mx}} and a minimum value of {{mn}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the amplitude.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the vertical translation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write a possible equation and describe the location of its maxima and minima over two cycles starting at $x=0$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Amplitude $a=\dfrac{ {{mx}}-({{mn}}) }{2}={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}$.

(b) Vertical translation $c=\dfrac{ {{mx}}+({{mn}}) }{2}={{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

(c) $y={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}\cos x+({{(mx+mn)/2:3}})$ (period $2\pi$, no phase shift). Over two cycles, maxima at $x=0,2\pi,4\pi$; minima at $x=\pi,3\pi$.

rubric.point: Describes key points over two cycles

questions.text: One cycle of a sine function begins at $x=-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ and ends at $x=\frac{\pi}{ {{m}} }$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the phase shift.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the equation in the form $y=\sin[k(x-d)]$.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Period $=\frac{\pi}{ {{m}} }-\left(-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\right)=\pi\left(\frac{1}{ {{m}} }+\frac{1}{ {{n}} }\right)\approx{{pi*(1/m+1/n):3}}$.

(b) A sine cycle starts at a zero (going up), so the phase shift is $\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ to the left, $d=-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$.

(c) $k=\frac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2}{1/{{m}}+1/{{n}}}\approx{{2/(1/m+1/n):3}}$, so $y=\sin\left[{{2/(1/m+1/n):3}}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\right)\right]$.

rubric.point: Correct equation in the required form

questions.text: A musical note has a frequency of {{f}} Hz (cycles per second). The sound can be modelled by $y=\sin kt$, where $t$ is in seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the period of the note.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine $k$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain how the graph would change for a higher note.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Period $T=\dfrac1f=\dfrac{1}{ {{f}} }\approx{{1/f:3}}$ s.

(b) $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f=2\pi({{f}})\approx{{2*pi*f:4}}$.

(c) A higher note has a larger frequency, so a shorter period and a larger value of $k$; the graph is compressed horizontally.

rubric.point: Explains effect of higher pitch on period and k

questions.text: An electricity supply has a maximum voltage of {{V}} V and a frequency of {{f}} Hz.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the amplitude?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the period?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write an equation of the form $V=a\sin kt$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the location of the maxima, minima and zeros over two cycles.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Amplitude $={{V}}$ V.

(b) Period $=\dfrac{1}{ {{f}} }\approx{{1/f:3}}$ s.

(c) $k=2\pi({{f}})={{2*f}}\pi$, so $V={{V}}\sin({{2*f}}\pi t)$.

(d) Two cycles take $\frac{2}{ {{f}} }$ s; max {{V}} V at $t=\frac{T}{4}$ and $\frac{5T}{4}$, min $-{{V}}$ V at $\frac{3T}{4}$ and $\frac{7T}{4}$, zeros every half period.

rubric.point: Describes key points over two cycles

questions.text: An amusement-park ride completes one revolution every {{T}} s. Riders reach a maximum height of {{mx}} m and a minimum of {{mn}} m. The height is modelled by $h=a\sin(kt)+c$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the amplitude.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the vertical translation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What is the desired period?

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine $k$ and write the model.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $a=\dfrac{ {{mx}}-{{mn}} }{2}={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}$ m.

(b) $c=\dfrac{ {{mx}}+{{mn}} }{2}={{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$ m.

(c) The period should be {{T}} s (one revolution).

(d) $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }\approx{{2*pi/T:3}}$, so $h={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }t\right)+{{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

questions.text: A wave generator moves back and forth {{n}} complete cycles every minute, producing waves {{H}} m from crest to trough. Model the displacement $d$, in metres, of the water from its mean level at time $t$ seconds, assuming $d=0$ and rising at $t=0$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the amplitude.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the model.

parts.label: d
parts.text: How would the model change if the generator completed more cycles per minute?

questions.modelAnswer:
Period $T=\dfrac{60}{ {{n}} }={{60/n:3}}$ s, so $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi({{n}})}{60}\approx{{2*pi*n/60:3}}$.

Amplitude $=\dfrac{ {{H}} }{2}={{H/2:3}}$ m (crest to trough is twice the amplitude).

Model: $d={{H/2:3}}\sin({{2*pi*n/60:3}}\,t)$.

If the generator speeds up, the period becomes shorter (k larger); the amplitude would only change if the wave height changes.

rubric.point: Amplitude is half the crest-to-trough height

questions.text: Compare the graphs of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\cos x$. Explain how a phase shift maps the sine function onto the cosine function, and explain why there is more than one phase shift that works.
questions.modelAnswer:
Both graphs have the same shape, amplitude 1, period $2\pi$ and range $[-1,1]$. The sine graph starts at $(0,0)$ going up; the cosine graph starts at its maximum $(0,1)$.

Shifting $y=\sin x$ to the **left** by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ moves its maximum from $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ to $x=0$, giving $y=\cos x$: $\cos x=\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

Because the graphs repeat every $2\pi$, adding any multiple of $2\pi$ to the shift also works, e.g. a shift of $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ to the right: $\cos x=\sin\left(x-\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)$.

rubric.point: Correct shift π/2 left with explanation
Explains periodicity gives other shifts, with an example

questions.text: Use the quotient identity $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and the graphs of sine and cosine to explain (a) where $y=\tan x$ has zeros, (b) where it has vertical asymptotes, (c) why it is positive on $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and negative on $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$, and (d) why its period is $\pi$.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A fraction is zero when its numerator is zero: $\sin x=0$ at $x=0,\pi,2\pi,\dots$, so $\tan x$ has zeros there.

(b) The fraction is undefined when the denominator is zero: $\cos x=0$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2},\dots$ As $\cos x\to0$ the quotient grows without bound, giving vertical asymptotes.

(c) On $\left(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ both sine and cosine are positive, so the quotient is positive. On $\left(\frac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$ sine is positive and cosine negative, so tangent is negative.

(d) After a half-turn ($\pi$) both sine and cosine change sign: $\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x$, $\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x$, so their quotient is unchanged. The pattern of tangent values repeats every $\pi$.

rubric.point: Asymptotes from denominator with explanation of unbounded growth

questions.text: A function is **even** if $f(-x)=f(x)$ and **odd** if $f(-x)=-f(x)$. Determine whether $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$ and $y=\tan x$ are even, odd or neither. Justify each answer using the graphs or the unit circle.
questions.modelAnswer:
On the unit circle, the angle $-x$ is the reflection of $x$ in the $x$-axis: the $x$-coordinate is unchanged and the $y$-coordinate changes sign.

* $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$: **odd**; the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin.
* $\cos(-x)=\cos x$: **even**; the graph is symmetric in the $y$-axis.
* $\tan(-x)=\dfrac{\sin(-x)}{\cos(-x)}=\dfrac{-\sin x}{\cos x}=-\tan x$: **odd**.

rubric.point: Correct classification of sine with justification
Correct classification of cosine with justification
Correct classification of tangent with justification

questions.text: State the key features of $y=\tan x$ on $[0,2\pi]$: maximum/minimum, amplitude, period, zeros, $y$-intercept, equations of the vertical asymptotes, domain and range. Explain what happens to $\tan x$ as $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^-$ and as $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^+$.
questions.modelAnswer:
No maximum or minimum, so no amplitude. Period $\pi$. Zeros $0,\pi,2\pi$. $y$-intercept $0$. Asymptotes $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\frac{3\pi}{2}$. Domain $\{x\in\mathbb R\mid x\ne\frac{\pi}{2}+n\pi\}$, range $\mathbb R$.

As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^-$, $\sin x\to1$ and $\cos x\to0$ through positive values, so $\tan x\to+\infty$. As $x\to\frac{\pi}{2}^+$, $\cos x\to0$ through negative values, so $\tan x\to-\infty$.

rubric.point: Behaviour near π/2 from both sides with reasons

questions.text:
The graph of a cosine function is shown.

```plot
f: {{a}}*cos({{k}}*x)+{{c}}
domain: -pi, 2*pi
xticks: pi
```

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the maximum and minimum values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the amplitude.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the vertical translation.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Determine the period.

parts.label: e
parts.text: What value of $k$ gives this period?

parts.label: f
parts.text: Explain why the phase shift can have more than one value, and suggest three possible values.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Max $={{a+c}}$, min $={{c-a}}$.

(b) Amplitude $=\dfrac{ {{a+c}}-({{c-a}}) }{2}={{a}}$.

(c) Vertical translation $=\dfrac{ {{a+c}}+({{c-a}}) }{2}={{c}}$.

(d) Consecutive maxima are $\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }$ apart, so the period is $\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }\approx{{2*pi/k:3}}$.

(e) $k=\frac{2\pi}{T}={{k}}$.

(f) A cosine graph has a maximum at every $x=\frac{2\pi n}{ {{k}} }$, so a phase shift of $0$, $\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }$, or $-\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }$ (any whole number of periods) all produce the same graph.

rubric.point: Explains why phase shift is not unique and gives three values

questions.text:
Consider the relation $y=\lvert\sin x\rvert$ on $[-2\pi,2\pi]$.

```plot
f: abs(sin(x))
domain: -2*pi, 2*pi
range: -1.5, 1.5
xticks: pi
```

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the shape of the graph and how it relates to $y=\sin x$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the maximum, minimum and period.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Is the relation a function? Justify.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Is it even, odd or neither? Justify.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Every negative part of the sine curve is reflected above the $x$-axis, giving a series of identical 'arches' that touch the $x$-axis at multiples of $\pi$.

(b) Maximum 1, minimum 0, period $\pi$ (one arch).

(c) It is a function: each $x$ gives exactly one $y$ value (any vertical line meets the graph once).

(d) $\lvert\sin(-x)\rvert=\lvert-\sin x\rvert=\lvert\sin x\rvert$, so the relation is **even**.

questions.text: Create your own description of a sinusoidal function that uses exactly one of each transformation from this section: a vertical translation, a change of amplitude, a phase shift, and a change of period – but apply them to **separate** functions $y=\sin x+c$, $y=a\sin x$, $y=\sin(x-d)$ and $y=\sin kx$. For each, give your equation, a clue a classmate could use to identify it, and the key points of one cycle.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sample answer:

* $y=\sin x+3$: clue 'max 4, min 2'. Key points $(0,3),(\frac{\pi}{2},4),(\pi,3),(\frac{3\pi}{2},2),(2\pi,3)$.
* $y=-2\sin x$: clue 'amplitude 2, reflected'. Key points $(0,0),(\frac{\pi}{2},-2),(\pi,0),(\frac{3\pi}{2},2),(2\pi,0)$.
* $y=\sin(x-\frac{\pi}{3})$: clue 'first zero going up at $\frac{\pi}{3}$'. Key points shift right $\frac{\pi}{3}$.
* $y=\sin3x$: clue 'period $\frac{2\pi}{3}$'. Key points at $0,\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{2\pi}{3}$.

Marking looks for correct, consistent clues and key points rather than particular numbers.

rubric.point: Four correct equations of the stated forms
Clues that uniquely identify each transformation

questions.text:
Consider the line $y=\frac{x}{ {{n}} }$ and the curve $y=\sin x$ graphed on the same axes with no restriction on the domain.

```plot
f: sin(x)
f: x/{{n}} | dashed
domain: -{{n+1}}, {{n+1}}
range: -1.5, 1.5
```

parts.label: a
parts.text: How many times do the graphs intersect? Justify your answer.

questions.modelAnswer:
The sine curve stays between $-1$ and $1$, so intersections can only occur where $-1\le\frac{x}{ {{n}} }\le1$, i.e. $-{{n}}\le x\le {{n}}$.

Both graphs are odd, so intersections are symmetric about the origin, and $(0,0)$ is one of them.

For $0<x\le{{n}}$: the line meets the first arch (on $(0,\pi)$) once. On $(\pi,2\pi)$ sine is negative while the line is positive, so there are no intersections. The next positive arch peaks at $x=2\pi+\frac{\pi}{2}\approx7.85$. The line crosses that arch (twice) only if it is still below 1 there, i.e. only if ${{n}}>7.85$.

Total: {{tot}} intersections ({{(tot-1)/2}} for $x>0$, the same number for $x<0$, plus the origin).

A good answer explains the bounding argument, the symmetry, and counts carefully using the graph.

rubric.point: Uses −1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1 to bound the region of intersection
Counts intersections correctly for the given line with justification
